steps.say: Search in an AI application runs on an embedding model. It turns the question and every document into vectors, and the search returns the closest documents.
A large embedding model ranks results well, but it needs more memory and more time for every search.
A small model, here with 22.7 million parameters, runs on an ordinary computer. That suits organizations with limited computing.
steps.speak: A small model, here with twenty-two point seven million parameters, runs on an ordinary computer. That suits organizations with limited computing.

steps.say: GISTEmbed trains the small model with the large model as its guide.
steps.speak: Gist Embed trains the small model with the large model as its guide.

steps.say: A search model learns from pairs: a query and a text that answers it. Training takes a batch of such pairs.
For each query, training pulls the matching text closer in the model's space of meaning.
Every other text in the batch is pushed away, as a negative. These negatives need no labelling, which is why training at scale uses them.
Some of those texts are related to the query. A sentence on Canberra, the capital of Australia, sits in another pair of the batch.
Pushed away as a negative, it teaches the model that capital cities and Canberra are unrelated, which is the opposite of what search needs.
Training sets are too large to check by hand. One that the paper uses holds 1.45 million examples.
steps.speak: Training sets are too large to check by hand. One that the paper uses holds one point four five million examples.

steps.say: GISTEmbed adds a guide: a large embedding model that scores every text in the batch against the query.
steps.speak: Gist Embed adds a guide: a large embedding model that scores every text in the batch against the query.

steps.say: The pair itself sets the bar. The guide scores capital cities and Ottawa at 0.65.
steps.speak: The pair itself sets the bar. The guide scores capital cities and Ottawa at zero point six five.

steps.say: Two texts score above it: the sentence on Canberra and the question about the capital of Australia.
A text that the guide scores above the pair is left out of the negatives for that query.
The other texts stay as negatives. The rule adds no setting to tune, and it runs for every query in every batch.
The small model is then no longer pushed away from texts that answer the query.
The small model learns from the negatives that remain.
The guide runs only during training. Search then uses the small model alone, at its own size and speed.
On a benchmark of 56 tasks, the small model scored 56.3 before this training.
steps.speak: On a benchmark of fifty-six tasks, the small model scored fifty-six point three before this training.

steps.say: Training without a guide raised the score to 57.5. Training with GISTEmbed raised it to 58.1.
steps.speak: Training without a guide raised the score to fifty-seven point five. Training with Gist Embed raised it to fifty-eight point one.

steps.say: On search tasks, the score rose from 42.0 to 44.4. In the paper, the smallest models gained the most.
steps.speak: On search tasks, the score rose from forty-two to forty-four point four. In the paper, the smallest models gained the most.

steps.say: The guide's own errors carry over into training.
Results also depend on the training data. For the larger models, search scores fell on some tasks that the training data hardly covered.
The method needs only pairs of a query and a matching text, so an organization can train a small search model on its own pairs.
Sentence Transformers implements this method as GISTEmbedLoss.
steps.speak: Sentence Transformers implements this method as Gist Embed Loss.
